12.0.0.en: It is not expedient for me to glory: it is not right for a Christian or a servant to boast of himself, for this is a kind of pride; but Paul was compelled to do so in defense of his ministry, so that the Corinthians would not doubt his teaching and the Gospel he preached to them.

12.0.2.en: Revelations: a voice from heaven or an angel who explains and makes clear the will of God.

12.0.3.en: Paul ends his talk about the boasting to which he was compelled, and moves on to another subject, namely the work of God that appears in visions and revelations from heaven to encourage His children; and in this there is no glory for man.

12.1.0.en: A man: he means himself, but out of humility he did not say that it was he, so that he might teach us to be humble and not to proclaim our personal experiences with pride, but, if we are compelled, to hide ourselves so that God may be glorified. In Christ: a believer in Christ who lives a spiritual life with Him.

12.1.1.en: In the body: with his body.

12.1.2.en: Out of the body: with his spirit alone.

12.1.3.en: The third heaven: the first heaven is the heaven of the birds, the second heaven is the heaven of the stars, and the third heaven is where the angels and the saints dwell, that is, Paradise and the Kingdom. Here Paul declares a vision that he had seen fourteen years before the writing of this Epistle, that is, in the year AD 43. Because of the greatness and power of the vision, he declares his inability to determine whether he saw it in his spirit alone, or whether God lifted him up to heaven in his spirit and body to see the glories of Paradise.

12.2.0.en: Paradise: a word of Persian origin meaning a garden. Paradise is the place where the righteous wait until the day of judgment, when He will transfer them to the Kingdom. It is called the Paradise of bliss or of joy because the state of the spirits there is one of joy and bliss.

12.2.1.en: Not lawful: no man is able to express them, because they are beyond words and imagination.

12.2.2.en: Paul declares that he saw great things in Paradise which cannot be expressed, because they are higher than all human conceptions.

12.3.0.en: Paul affirms that boasting is to be in the grace of God, as it appeared in this vision, and not in man's works and achievements. So he does not boast of anything, and if he is compelled, he will boast of his shortcomings and weaknesses, which Christ completes; that is, he boasts only in the grace of God, while keeping his humility.

12.4.0.en: Paul shows that if he speaks of things he has accomplished, this is not foolishness, because he is truthful in every word and was compelled to do so in order to confirm his teaching and preaching. But he returns and affirms that he avoids boasting needlessly, lest he show himself great and be proud in the eyes of others; he does not desire that, but only to confirm and establish his teaching. That is, he is able at any time to show his abilities and distinction, but he will not do this, so as not to fall into pride; for his way, and the way of all Christians, is humility and the hiding of virtues.

12.4.1.en: Do not show your superiority over others, but praise them and encourage them; and if they praise you, direct your thanks to God, so that pride does not war against you.

12.5.1.en: The revelations: the visions and the gifts.

12.5.2.en: A thorn in the flesh: an illness.

12.5.3.en: The messenger of Satan: Satan wanted to hinder Paul from the ministry and to harm him, and God permitted it for his benefit, so that he might keep his humility.

12.5.4.en: To buffet me: to mistreat me.

12.5.5.en: Paul declared the grace of God toward him through an illness that God permitted, namely a weakness in the eyes (Gal 4:15), which forced him to dictate his epistles to others, and if he wrote anything himself he wrote it in large letters (Gal 6:11); and also sores and pus that afflicted his body, on which he used to place pieces of cloth, and these soiled pieces of cloth used to heal the sick (Acts 19:12). It is to be noted that the illness was lasting, because it was a constant protection for him from pride.

12.6.0.en: Paul declares that he prayed three times that God would heal him of his illness; and because his prayer was made in reliance and surrender to God, He declared to him that he should not ask again, because this illness was by His permission for his benefit, and that the grace of God would support him and suffice for all his needs, so that he would not be hindered in anything in his life or ministry. Rather, He declared to him something more than this: that his bodily weakness would not make him weak in anything, but his strength would be made perfect by the grace of God, so that he became joyful and proud of this illness because it was a constant cause for the power of God to work in him. Thus Paul experienced God every day through His making up for what he lacked and helping him to live, and he became not like the rest but better than they, because he was made perfect by the power of God.

12.7.0.en: Here Paul repeats his joy in his weakness and in everything that befalls him of persecutions, whether insults and abuse, or poverty, or any suffering for the sake of Christ, because through them he experiences the work of God in him. For when he feels his weakness and humbles himself before God, he immediately becomes strong through His support of him.

12.7.1.en: Do not be distressed by your weakness or your troubles, because they are your way to enjoy the work of God in you. Accept them with thanksgiving, and be humble and lowly before Him, and the divine blessings will pour down upon you and you will become distinguished from those around you.

12.8.0.en: Paul affirms that boasting of personal achievements is folly, but the Corinthians compelled him to do this, because they did not defend him before the false teachers who boasted of themselves and cast doubt on his apostleship and teaching, but kept silent; and this was weakness and sin on their part, especially since Paul's ministry is no less than the ministry and preaching of the outstanding Apostles, namely Peter, James and John. But Paul feels within himself that he is nothing, and he says all this for the benefit of his hearers, so that they may stand firm in the teachings of Christ which he preached to them.

12.9.0.en: Here Paul proves his apostleship by the miracles he performed in the Church of Corinth, while he was suffering tribulations and persecutions from them; therefore they ought to have believed in his apostleship and teaching, and not been disturbed and believed the doubts raised by the opponents.

12.10.0.en: Paul asks the Corinthians in reproach what was lacking in his preaching to them and his care, for their church received complete care like the rest of the churches that the other Apostles founded. Then he shames them by saying that he did lack one thing for them, namely not burdening them with paying for his living expenses, and he did this so that they would not say that he asked a reward for his ministry among them. And he corrects himself and asks them to forgive him for wronging them in this, since he deprived them of this grace, which is giving to the one who serves them; but he was compelled to do so lest they doubt his ministry, which he gave them free of charge.

12.11.0.en: It is understood from this verse that before writing this Epistle Paul had visited Corinth twice, and he declares his readiness to visit them a third time and to serve them without material payment, and there are two reasons for this:

12.11.1.en: 1- That he loves them and seeks their salvation, not their money and their gifts.

12.11.2.en: 2- That he is a father, and it is the custom that fathers spend on their children for all their needs, and not the reverse, although when the fathers are in need the children must care for them.

12.12.0.en: I will gladly spend: I will give and offer what I have of money for your needs.

12.12.1.en: And be spent: I will give my life for your service.

12.12.2.en: Paul declares his joy in giving whatever money he possesses in the ministry, indeed in offering his life and giving it even to death for the preaching to and service of his children in Corinth. But it is very sad that the more love he showed them, the less love they showed him in return, that is, they doubt him and do not defend him before the opponents; and this is very hard on the heart of anyone who loves and sacrifices. By this he reproaches them gently, so that they may respond to his love and defend his preaching to them, and so stand firm in the faith.

12.13.0.en: But be it so: Paul accepts their weak love and continues to love them more and more.

12.13.1.en: Paul sent Titus and those with him to collect contributions for the poor of Jerusalem, and the opponents accused him of collecting these contributions in order to take from them for himself, and that he pretends to spend on his needs from the work of his hands and took nothing for himself from the church of Corinth, whereas in fact he does take, by means of what Titus collects; and this is a false accusation. But Paul says: if you accuse me of being crafty, then I am crafty for the sake of your salvation, and I caught you with guile when I offered a love that gave itself without return, to win your souls for Christ. This is the craftiness that he practiced, and not craftiness for the sake of material gain.

12.14.0.en: Paul affirms that he received nothing material from them, whether by himself or by means of his helpers such as Titus and those with him whom he sent to collect contributions for the needy believers in Jerusalem. Titus took nothing for himself, and none of his companions either, but they walked in the same manner as Paul in the ministry, that is, ministry free of charge.

12.15.0.en: Paul denies that by his previous words he wishes to display his righteousness and enjoy the praise of the Church of Corinth, because he feels that he is speaking before God, united with Christ who is in him, and intends only to establish them in the faith and in all the teachings he preached to them, so that this leads to the growth of their spiritual edification.

12.16.0.en: I shall not find you such as I wish: I find you walking in evil and not firm in the faith. And that I shall be found by you such as you do not wish: my rebuke and punishment will appear against those who persist in evil and in causing those around them to stumble.

12.16.1.en: Paul declares his fear that some of the believers in Corinth continue in evil, such as creating quarrels and factions, judging one another, and stirring up doubts and confusions that make many stumble, and a pride that leads to envy and anger, so that they depart from life with Christ.

12.17.0.en: Paul continues his fears that he may find many in the Church of Corinth still walking in evil, such as fornication connected with pride, and the quarrels mentioned in the previous verse; and this will grieve Paul very much and make him humbled before Satan, who made his children fall into these sins. But he will accept this from God, and will be moved and weep over them, and will try to admonish them and bring them back by repentance to God. He mentions this in the hope that it may stir the feelings of the believers who are firm in the faith, so that they may try to call these wicked ones to repentance before Paul comes.

12.17.1.en: Offer your love to others without waiting for their response to you, because God loves you, so you respond to Him with love for His children; and know that your love will bear its fruit in their hearts, even if after a while. But you will win the experience of God's mercies and the beholding of His love and the knowledge of Him.

12.17.2.en: Paul's warning and his call to the stubborn to repent

13.0.0.en: Paul visited Corinth in AD 53 (Acts 18:1-18), then visited it a second time in AD 56 (1 Cor 16:5-8), and he is about to visit them a third time, as he mentions here. He affirms his following words as a decision by which he judges the stubborn, and supports it with the testimony of two with him, as the Law of Moses requires, and these are Sosthenes (1 Cor 1:1) and Timothy (2 Cor 1:1), both of them disciples of Paul.

13.1.0.en: I have told you before: Paul declared that he would discipline the stubborn if they did not repent (ch. 10:

13.1.1.en: 2, ch. 12:21.) I say beforehand: before I come to you in Corinth I affirm that I shall punish the unrepentant.

13.1.2.en: The second time: the second visit to Corinth, which took place in AD 56.

13.1.3.en: All the rest: those who sinned and whose sins have not appeared or been exposed, or those who did not sin but are exposed to falling into fornication and stumbling sins.

13.1.4.en: Paul affirms with firmness and with his apostolic authority that he will punish those who persist in wrongdoing and refuse repentance when he visits them the third time. This shows the need for Church penalties when there is persistence in sin, such as depriving the offenders of fellowship in the Church, that is, of partaking of the Holy Mysteries.

13.2.0.en: A proof of Christ speaking: Paul's apostolic authority, which Christ gave him.

13.2.1.en: Here Paul affirms his apostolic authority which he received from Christ, because Christ is God and His authority is of utmost power; He is not weak before the stubborn, but strong and able to protect the Church, to establish the believers and to cut off the wicked until they repent.

13.3.0.en: Crucified through weakness: the crucified Christ appeared as a weak man, indeed in utmost humiliation and shame.

13.3.1.en: Lives by the power of God: He rose by His divinity, and He lives forever.

13.3.2.en: Weak in Him: the servants of Christ appear weak in what they endure for His sake during their ministry. We shall live with Him: we enjoy His fellowship and His work in us during our life on earth, so we are not disturbed by the insults and wrongs of others.

13.3.3.en: Toward you: we speak with authority, punish the offenders and hold fast to the firm teachings of Christ. The Apostle here again affirms his authority and strength in Christ; just as Christ appeared weak in His crucifixion, but in truth He is God, able to do all things, so we also appear weak in the insults and opposition we endure, but by the power of Christ we are able to lead the Church in the way of the Kingdom and to cut off the opponents.

13.3.4.en: Your strength has its source in Christ. So proclaim the truth with courage, whatever pressures you face. And if you endure insults, be sure that the truth that is in you is stronger than the evil that is in others. Do not doubt yourself, and pray for them, and surround your proclamation of the truth with love, so that people feel that you seek their good, and in the end submit to you for God's sake.

13.4.s.en: (2) Examination of the faith for the sake of repentance

13.4.0.en: Some believers of the Church of Corinth opposed Paul and tested him, doubting his apostleship, and here he calls them to examine themselves, whether they have the sound, living faith, or whether, because of their sins, they are rejected by Christ. What is required now is not to examine their teacher but to examine themselves, so that they may repent of their sins and walk in the upright faith. And the examination of the faith is not only making sure of religious beliefs, but also shows itself in spiritual fruits and is done under the guidance of the Fathers and spiritual guides.

13.5.0.en: Paul assures them that if they examine themselves in truth, they will discover that they are rejected by Christ because of their persistence in sin and their refusal to submit to the Church and its teachings, and they will then be certain that Paul and his helpers among the servants have the sound faith and are not rejected by Christ.

13.6.0.en: Paul shows the feelings of his tender fatherhood in his prayer for the Corinthians, that they may turn away from evil and do good, and so be righteous before God, not so that Paul may praise that his children are righteous, he who served them and preached to them so that they became so, but so that they may enjoy doing good and God's pleasure in them. Rather, his self-giving and love for them show that he is ready to appear as though rejected and in the wrong, so long as they are righteous; and he is not in truth rejected, but only seems to be rejected, as when it is said of him that he was more severe than he should have been and threatened them with punishment although they were righteous. He accepts being accused in this way, but what he desires is that they do good works that make them pleasing before God.

13.7.0.en: Paul affirms his adherence to the truth, who is God, in all his conduct and ministry; so he judges the offenders only by the truth, and if they repent he rejoices in them, and they become righteous before God.

13.8.0.en: We are weak: we do not mind appearing, for your sake, in the form of weakness.

13.8.1.en: You are strong: you walk well, keeping away from the former sins and rejecting them.

13.8.2.en: Your perfection: your striving toward Christian perfection.

13.8.3.en: Paul affirms his fatherhood in accepting the judgment of weakness and error against him, so that he may judge that his Corinthian children are strong and righteous; indeed he desires that they grow in their spiritual life until they become perfect.

13.9.0.en: Being absent: at the time of sending this Epistle, when he was staying in Macedonia.

13.9.1.en: Sharply: determining a penalty for the offenders and cutting them off from the Church.

13.9.2.en: Being present: in the midst of the Church of Corinth.

13.9.3.en: For edification and not for destruction: to help souls to live with God, and not as revenge or to destroy anyone. Paul declares that he uses his apostolic authority for edification, and that the purpose of warning sinners so that they repent is to be rid of carrying out any penalty on the offenders. His fatherhood desires that no one be punished and seeks the salvation of all.

13.9.4.en: Have a fatherhood toward all people, so that you forget yourself however much people wrong you, and seek their salvation, even if they are justified and their goodness appears before others, and at the same time you are accused of wrongdoing, even unjustly. What matters is that you draw all souls to God.

13.10.s.en: (3) Closing wishes and greeting of peace

13.10.0.en: Rejoice: in the fellowship of Christ and the Kingdom that awaits you.

13.10.2.en: Be of good comfort: by the work of the Holy Spirit in you and in the Church.

13.10.3.en: Be of one mind: care for unity of thought and opinion and keep away from factions and divisions.

13.10.4.en: Live in peace: be at peace with one another, even if that requires giving up some of your rights and bearing with one another.

13.10.5.en: At the close of the Epistle Paul shows his wishes for the believers in Corinth: joy, comfort, the enjoyment of peace, and the blessings of God which overflow upon those who walk in love and peace.

13.11.0.en: Since the first centuries Christians have been accustomed to greet and kiss one another as a sign of love and purity of heart, and the Church in the Divine Liturgy still calls her children to do this, so they greet one another by the touching of hands, men with men and women with women.

13.12.0.en: The saints: the believers who are sanctified in Christ and set apart for Him.

13.12.1.en: After Paul called them to peace with one another, he sends them the greeting of peace from the believers in the churches of Macedonia, where he is writing the Epistle.

13.13.0.en: Paul closes his Epistle with the blessing of the Holy Trinity: the Son, the Father and the Holy Spirit. He put the Son before the Father because through His redemption we obtained reconciliation with God, and then through the Holy Spirit we receive all the blessings of redemption in the Church. From this the Church has been accustomed to close her prayers with this blessing.

13.13.1.en: May you gladden the hearts of others with beautiful wishes, to encourage them and urge them to every good work.
